claims.text: LaFe13-xCoxSi1 is a magnetocaloric material.
Doping LaFe13-xCoxSi1 with 2 at.% aluminum will improve its magnetocaloric properties near room temperature.
The improvement will occur through an enhanced isothermal entropy change.
The enhanced isothermal entropy change will result from modifications to the crystal structure and magnetic exchange interactions.
The initial LaFe13-xCoxSi1 alloy is in a ferromagnetic state.
Aluminum is introduced at a concentration of 2 at.%.
The proposed operating and measurement range is 295–305 K and 0–5 T.
Substitutional aluminum doping is expected to alter the lattice parameters.
Substitutional aluminum doping is expected to alter magnetic exchange interactions.
X-ray diffraction and neutron scattering can be used to characterize the proposed structural changes.
Aluminum will substitute for iron in the alloy.
Substitution of aluminum for iron will alter the magnetic moment and exchange interactions.
Changes in magnetic moment and exchange interactions will enhance the magnetocaloric effect.
Studies and theoretical models on similar magnetocaloric materials show that non-rare-earth-element doping can modify magnetic properties and improve magnetocaloric performance.
The undoped alloy is assumed to have an isothermal entropy change of 3.75 J/kg·K.
Aluminum doping is predicted to increase the isothermal entropy change by 20% relative to the undoped alloy.
The doped alloy is predicted to have an isothermal entropy change of 4.5 J/kg·K.
The magnetocaloric effect in this class of materials is most pronounced at magnetic fields up to 5 T.
Sample preparation and measurement techniques may cause variation in measured isothermal entropy changes.
An increase of 0.5 J/kg·K corresponds to a 15% increase over the assumed baseline of 3.75 J/kg·K.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome specifies a 20% increase, equal to 0.75 J/kg·K from the stated 3.75 J/kg·K baseline, while the falsification rule accepts an increase of only 0.5 J/kg·K and labels it 15%. In fact, 0.5/3.75 is approximately 13.3%, so the prediction and decision threshold are quantitatively inconsistent.

The confidence-interval rule is logically inverted or incomplete: a confidence interval lying entirely above the threshold would not include the threshold, yet the stated rule would classify that result as falsifying the hypothesis.
